entries.label: CPTS arsenal
entries.detail: Command-first pentest reference, stripped to the tool level and organised by stage (Pre Compromise, Post Compromise Elevation, Miscellaneous): search by port, service or tool

entries.label: CPTS: Pre Compromise
entries.detail: From an in-scope network to a user-level foothold: discover and enumerate the services, attack the ones that face you, enumerate the domain, and turn a web app, a weak login or captured authentication into your first shell or credential.

entries.label: CPTS: Post Compromise Elevation
entries.detail: Once you are on a box: enumerate the host, escalate to SYSTEM or root, dump the local and domain credential stores, abuse AD rights and delegation, and reuse what you find to move and climb towards full control.

entries.label: CPTS: Miscellaneous
entries.detail: The cross-cutting plumbing of an engagement: catch and stabilise shells, move files on and off a host, generate payloads, tunnel through a foothold, build wordlists and crack the hashes you capture offline.

entries.label: Active Directory enumeration: Mapping the domain
entries.detail: Once you have any domain credential, map users, groups, computers, GPOs, trusts and the password policy. The data that drives every AD attack path.
entries.words: From Linux, with a credential From Windows, with PowerView What to look for Notes

entries.label: Attacking common applications: WordPress, Tomcat, Jenkins, GitLab
entries.detail: The off-the-shelf apps that turn up on internal web ports and the quick route to code execution on each. Fingerprint the app, try default and weak credentials, then use the admin feature that runs code: a theme editor, a WAR deploy, a script console.
entries.words: Fingerprint first WordPress Tomcat Jenkins GitLab / Drupal / Joomla Splunk, PRTG, osTicket, ColdFusion Notes

entries.label: Attacking common services: FTP, SMB, SQL, RDP, DNS and email attacks
entries.detail: Past enumeration: turning an open service into access. Anonymous and brute-forced logins, SQL command execution, RDP session hijack, DNS zone transfers, and SMTP user enumeration and relay. The attack side of the services you found on the port scan.
entries.words: When to reach for it FTP (21) SMB (445) SQL: MSSQL (1433) & MySQL (3306) RDP (3389) DNS (53) Email (25/110/143/587) Notes

entries.label: AutoRecon: Automated recon orchestration
entries.detail: A multi-target recon orchestrator. It runs the port scan, then fires the right enumeration tool at each service it finds and files the output per host and port. Use it to get broad, structured coverage early so you can read while it works.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: BloodHound: Active Directory attack paths
entries.detail: Maps Active Directory as a graph and finds the shortest path from where you are to Domain Admin. A collector (SharpHound or the Python collector) gathers users, groups, sessions, ACLs and trusts; BloodHound shows who can reach what, and how.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: bloodhound-python: Collecting BloodHound data from Linux
entries.detail: The Python BloodHound collector. From Linux, with any domain credential, it gathers users, groups, ACLs, sessions and trusts over LDAP and SMB and writes the JSON zip you load into BloodHound. The way to map a domain's attack paths when you have no Windows foothold to run SharpHound on.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Certipy: AD CS enumeration and abuse
entries.detail: Finds and abuses misconfigured Active Directory Certificate Services. Enumerate the CA and its templates, spot the ESC flaws, then request a certificate as another user and turn it into their hash or a Kerberos ticket. The go-to for ADCS paths once you have any domain account.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Database attacks: MSSQL and MySQL from a login
entries.detail: Once you have a database login, turn it into command execution and credentials. On MSSQL that means xp_cmdshell, impersonation and linked servers; on MySQL, reading files and writing a web shell. The database is often the shortest path from a weak credential to a shell.
entries.words: When to reach for it MSSQL MySQL Workflow Notes

entries.label: DNS enumeration: Records, subdomains and zone transfers
entries.detail: Pulling structure out of DNS: resolve the standard records, try a zone transfer that hands you the whole zone at once, and brute-force subdomains when it does not. A misconfigured DNS server leaking its zone is one of the fastest wins in external and internal enumeration.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: enum4linux-ng: All-in-one SMB and RPC enumeration
entries.detail: A rewrite of the classic enum4linux that fires every useful SMB/RPC enumeration at a host and files the results — users, groups, shares, the password policy, OS info and RID-cycled accounts — in one command. The quickest way to turn an open 445 into a full picture of a Windows or Samba host.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: feroxbuster: Recursive web content discovery
entries.detail: A fast, recursive directory and file brute-forcer. It walks into every directory it finds and keeps scanning, so a single run maps a whole site. Reach for it when a web port is open and gobuster or ffuf is leaving depth unexplored.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: ffuf: Web fuzzing
entries.detail: A fast web fuzzer that puts the FUZZ keyword anywhere in a request: paths, parameters, headers, POST bodies and Host for vhosts. The flexible companion to Gobuster when you need recursion, filtering or to fuzz something other than a path.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Gobuster: Web content discovery
entries.detail: Brute-forces hidden web content: directories and files, DNS subdomains, and virtual hosts. Run it against any HTTP or HTTPS service once a port scan finds one.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Hydra: Credential attacks
entries.detail: Online password guessing against a live service: SSH, FTP, RDP, web login forms and many more. Use it for a targeted spray with a short, sensible list, not a blind dictionary run.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Kerberos attacks: Roasting, delegation and ticket abuse
entries.detail: Turning Kerberos into credentials and access: roast service and pre-auth-less accounts for offline cracking, then reuse tickets to move and persist. The core of the AD domain phase.
entries.words: Kerberoasting (service accounts) AS-REP roasting (no pre-auth) Pass / overpass the hash, and tickets Windows, with Rubeus Notes

entries.label: Kerbrute: Kerberos user enumeration and spraying
entries.detail: Validates Active Directory usernames fast and quietly against the KDC (a bad username draws no logon failure), then sprays one password across the accounts that exist. The first move when you have a domain and a user list but no credentials yet.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: ldapsearch: LDAP and AD enumeration
entries.detail: Queries a domain controller's directory over LDAP. Anonymous, it often leaks the naming context and the domain's basic shape; with any credential it dumps users, groups, computers, descriptions and account flags. The low-level read behind BloodHound and NetExec, handy when you want the raw objects.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Manual SQL injection: Auth bypass, UNION, blind and file access
entries.detail: Doing by hand what sqlmap automates: break out of the query, bypass a login, pull data with UNION, read it blind when there is no output, enumerate the database through information_schema, and read or write files. The fundamentals that tell you when and how to point sqlmap, or finish the job it cannot.
entries.words: When to reach for it Spot it and break out Authentication bypass UNION-based extraction Error-based and blind Enumerate the database Read and write files Notes

entries.label: mitm6: IPv6 DNS takeover and relay
entries.detail: Abuses the fact that Windows prefers IPv6 and asks for a DHCPv6 lease nobody answers. mitm6 answers, becomes the clients' DNS server, and poisons name lookups (classically WPAD) to coerce authentication, which you relay with ntlmrelayx to LDAP or SMB. The quiet IPv6 cousin of Responder, and a reliable first move in a default AD network.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: NetExec: Network and AD enumeration
entries.detail: The successor to CrackMapExec. Sweeps a subnet for SMB, WinRM, LDAP, MSSQL and more, checks credentials across hosts, lists shares and users, and flags where a credential is a local admin. The workhorse of internal and Active Directory enumeration.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: NFS enumeration: Exports, mounts and no_root_squash
entries.detail: Lists a host's NFS exports, mounts the ones you can reach, and reads or writes the files inside. A misconfigured export — world-readable data, or the dangerous no_root_squash — turns a network share into file access and sometimes a direct route to root.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Nikto: Web server vulnerability scan
entries.detail: A fast, noisy web server scanner. It checks for dangerous files, outdated software, misconfigurations, default pages and known CGI flaws, and prints the server banner and anything interesting it stumbles on. A good first sweep of a web port before you go hunting by hand.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Nmap: Network scanning
entries.detail: The port scanner. Finds live hosts, open ports, service versions and, through NSE scripts, a first pass of service enumeration. Usually the first command run against an in-scope network.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: NTLM relay and coercion: Relaying captured authentication
entries.detail: When a machine or user authenticates to you, forward that authentication straight to another host instead of cracking it. Pair ntlmrelayx with a coercion (PetitPotam, printer bug, Coercer) to make a target authenticate on demand. The route to a shell, a hash dump or an ADCS certificate from one captured NTLM.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Packet capture (tcpdump & Wireshark): Sniffing credentials off the wire
entries.detail: Capturing and reading network traffic to pull out the secrets that cross it in the clear — FTP, Telnet, HTTP basic auth, SNMP community strings, and protocol handshakes. tcpdump grabs the packets on a foothold, Wireshark (or net-creds) reads them. Free credentials when a protocol was never encrypted.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: PowerUpSQL: Discovering and attacking MSSQL in a domain
entries.detail: Finds every SQL Server in a domain from its SPNs, checks where your account can log in, audits each instance for privilege-escalation paths, and crawls linked-server chains to run commands on boxes you were never meant to reach. The PowerShell toolkit that turns a domain foothold into MSSQL compromise.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Responder: LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning
entries.detail: Answers LLMNR, NBT-NS and mDNS name-resolution requests on the local segment, so a host looking for a mistyped or missing name connects to you instead and hands over an NTLMv2 hash. A top source of first credentials on an internal test.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: rpcclient: MSRPC enumeration over SMB
entries.detail: Talks to the Windows (or Samba) MSRPC interfaces over SMB. With a null or valid session it enumerates users, groups, shares, the password policy and more, and RID-cycles to turn one known account into the whole user list. A classic first move against 139/445 before you have credentials.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: RustScan: Fast port scanning
entries.detail: A very fast port sweep that finds the open ports in seconds, then hands them straight to Nmap for version and script scanning. Use it as the front end to Nmap when a full-range scan would otherwise be slow.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: SearchSploit: Exploit lookup (Exploit-DB)
entries.detail: The command-line search for the offline Exploit-DB archive. Match a service and version from recon to a known public exploit, read it, and copy it out to work on. The bridge from "what version is this" to "is there an exploit".
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Service enumeration: Port by port enumeration cheat sheet
entries.detail: After the port scan, the first move on each open service. What to run against FTP, SSH, SMTP, DNS, SMB, SNMP, LDAP, MSSQL, NFS and the rest to pull users, shares, versions and config.
entries.words: FTP (21), SSH (22), SMTP (25) DNS (53) SMB (139/445) and RPC SNMP (161/udp), LDAP (389) NFS (2049), MSSQL (1433), MySQL (3306), RDP (3389), WinRM (5985) Oracle TNS (1521), IPMI (623), rsync (873) Notes

entries.label: SMB enumeration: Shares, users and RPC on 139/445
entries.detail: SMB is the richest target on a Windows network. Try a null or guest session first, then list shares, read what is readable, pull the user and group list over RPC and note the password policy. The usual source of the first foothold or the first credential.
entries.words: When to reach for it Null / guest first Shares: list, then read Users, groups and policy over RPC If enumdomusers is blocked: RID cycling Notes

entries.label: smbclient, smbmap & enum4linux: SMB client tools (connect, list, read)
entries.detail: The command-line SMB clients you reach for over 139/445: smbclient for an interactive session, smbmap for a fast read/write permission map, enum4linux-ng for a full rollup, and smbget to pull files. The tools behind the SMB enumeration workflow.
entries.words: When to reach for it enum4linux-ng (the rollup) smbmap (permission map) smbclient (interactive) and smbget Notes

entries.label: smtp-user-enum: Validating usernames over SMTP
entries.detail: Asks a mail server whether a username exists using the SMTP verbs VRFY, EXPN and RCPT TO. A server that answers differently for valid and invalid users hands you a verified account list to spray or feed into other services — a quiet win from an open port 25.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: SNMP enumeration: Community strings on 161/udp
entries.detail: SNMP on UDP 161 is easy to miss and often wide open with a default community string. Guess the string, then walk the MIB for running processes, users, network shares, software and sometimes credentials in plaintext. A quiet source of host detail and the occasional password.
entries.words: When to reach for it Find a valid community string Walk the tree Notes

entries.label: sqlmap: SQL injection
entries.detail: Automates finding and exploiting SQL injection. Confirms the flaw, fingerprints the database, dumps data, and: where the configuration allows: reads files or gets command execution. Point it at a request you suspect is injectable.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Web attacks: LFI, upload, command injection, SSTI
entries.detail: The web flaws that turn a page into code execution or file read, beyond SQL injection. Local and remote file inclusion, upload bypasses, command injection and template injection, with the payloads to confirm each.
entries.words: Local / remote file inclusion (LFI/RFI) File upload bypass Command injection Server-side template injection (SSTI) Notes

entries.label: Web proxies (Burp & ZAP): Intercept, repeat, fuzz and encode HTTP
entries.detail: An intercepting proxy sits between the browser and the app so you can read, edit and replay every request. Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP are the two to know: intercept and tamper, replay in Repeater, brute positions in Intruder, and encode or decode payloads. The backbone of hands-on web testing.
entries.words: When to reach for it Set up the proxy Proxy other tools through Burp Repeater and Intruder Decode and encode (Decoder / Inspector) OWASP ZAP Notes

entries.label: Web recon and fingerprinting: Identify the stack before you attack it
entries.detail: Before fuzzing or exploiting a web app, learn what it is: server, framework, CMS, versions and any WAF in the way. whatweb and the response headers name the stack, nikto flags the obvious misconfigurations, and nuclei matches it against a library of known issues.
entries.words: When to reach for it Fingerprint the stack Scan for known issues Also check by hand Notes

entries.label: WPScan: WordPress enumeration and attack
entries.detail: The dedicated WordPress scanner. It fingerprints the core version, enumerates plugins, themes and users, flags known vulnerabilities, and brute-forces logins against the xmlrpc or wp-login endpoint. WordPress is everywhere on internal web ports, and a vulnerable plugin is a common route to code execution.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: XSS, SSRF and XXE: Injection beyond the shell
entries.detail: The web flaws that do not hand you a shell but still win: run script in a victim's browser, make the server fetch what you cannot reach, or read files and reach internal hosts through a hungry XML parser. The payloads to confirm each and turn it into impact.
entries.words: Cross-site scripting (XSS) Server-side request forgery (SSRF) XML external entity (XXE) Notes

entries.label: Active Directory ACL abuse: Turning a BloodHound edge into access
entries.detail: BloodHound shows an edge like GenericAll or WriteDACL from your account to another object. ACL abuse is how you spend it: reset a password, add yourself to a group, grant delegation or write a shadow credential. The glue between an attack path and actual access.
entries.words: When to reach for it The common edges and their moves From Linux (impacket / bloodyAD) From Windows (PowerView) Notes

entries.label: Certify: AD CS enumeration and abuse (Windows)
entries.detail: The Windows counterpart to Certipy: find and abuse misconfigured Active Directory Certificate Services from a domain-joined foothold. Enumerate the CA and its templates, spot the ESC flaws, then request a certificate as another user and turn it into their Kerberos TGT. The on-host path to escalation and persistence through AD CS.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Credential hunting: Finding passwords already on the box
entries.detail: The next account is usually sitting on the one you own: in a config file, a script, a history file, a saved session or the registry. Hunt it before you reach for an exploit. A reused password here is the quiet path to lateral movement.
entries.words: When to reach for it Linux Windows Find interesting files by type Automate Notes

entries.label: Domain trust attacks: Crossing domains and forests
entries.detail: Domain Admin on one domain is rarely the end. Trusts link domains and forests, and a trust you can abuse carries your access across the boundary. Enumerate the trusts, then ride a child-to-parent SID-history path or a forest trust key to the next domain.
entries.words: When to reach for it Enumerate the trusts first Child to parent, within a forest (ExtraSids) Across a forest trust Notes

entries.label: Evil-WinRM: Remote access (WinRM)
entries.detail: A clean interactive shell over WinRM (Windows Remote Management). Give it a password or an NTLM hash and, if the account is in Remote Management Users, you get a PowerShell session with handy upload, download and in-memory script loading built in.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: gMSADumper: Reading gMSA managed passwords
entries.detail: Reads the managed password of a Group Managed Service Account over LDAP, when your principal is allowed to retrieve it. gMSA passwords are long and auto-rotated, so nobody types them — but the accounts often have strong rights, and the NTLM hash it returns is immediately usable for Pass-the-Hash and onward escalation.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Impacket: Windows and AD protocol tooling
entries.detail: A toolbox of Python scripts that speak Windows protocols directly. secretsdump pulls hashes, the exec scripts (psexec, wmiexec) give remote shells, and GetUserSPNs/GetNPUsers pull Kerberos tickets to crack. The backbone of Active Directory attacks from Linux.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: KeyTabExtract: Pulling hashes out of Kerberos keytab files
entries.detail: A keytab file on a domain-joined Linux host stores the keys an account uses to authenticate with Kerberos. KeyTabExtract reads a .keytab and recovers the NTLM and AES keys inside — so a keytab you can read turns into a Pass-the-Hash, a forged ticket, or a hash to crack for the plaintext password.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: LaZagne: Recovering stored credentials on a host
entries.detail: Pulls saved passwords out of the software already on a compromised host — browsers, mail clients, Wi-Fi, databases, chats, sysadmin tools and the Windows Credential Manager. One command recovers the reused passwords that move you laterally, without touching LSASS or the SAM.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Linikatz: Mimikatz for domain-joined UNIX
entries.detail: Cisco's answer to Mimikatz for UNIX hosts integrated with Active Directory. Run as root, it sweeps every common integration — SSSD, FreeIPA, Samba, Winbind, Vintela — and pulls out the Kerberos material each one caches: ccache files, keytabs, machine secrets and cached hashes, dropped into a folder ready to reuse.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Linux privilege escalation: Local root on Linux
entries.detail: The checks that turn a user shell into root: sudo rights, SUID binaries, cron jobs, capabilities, writable files and PATH. Run the enumeration, then exploit the one good finding.
entries.words: Enumerate Common wins SUID/SGID and capabilities, in depth Notes

entries.label: linux-exploit-suggester: Matching the kernel to known exploits
entries.detail: Reads the kernel version and userland of a Linux host and lists the public privilege-escalation exploits likely to work against it, with a rough probability and links. The quick triage for "is this box vulnerable to a known kernel bug" when a clean misconfiguration privesc is not on offer.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: mimikatz: Windows credential dumping
entries.detail: The credential toolkit on Windows. Pull plaintext, hashes and Kerberos tickets from LSASS, dump the local SAM, DCSync a hash straight from a domain controller, and pass or forge tickets. Reach for it once you have admin on a Windows host.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: mimipenguin: Dumping cleartext credentials from Linux memory
entries.detail: The Linux answer to Mimikatz's cleartext dump. With root, it scrapes the memory of processes that hold a user's password — the display manager, sshd, sudo, VSFTPd — and recovers the plaintext. A quick way to turn a fresh root shell into the actual password behind it, ready to reuse elsewhere.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Pass the Certificate: Turning an X.509 certificate into a Kerberos TGT
entries.detail: PKINIT lets Kerberos authenticate with a certificate instead of a password, so any X.509 certificate for an account — minted from an AD CS misconfiguration, an ESC8 relay or a Shadow Credential — can be exchanged for that account's TGT. Once you hold the ticket you are back in Pass-the-Ticket territory: DCSync, Evil-WinRM, the lot.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key tools and flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Pass the Ticket (Linux): Abusing Kerberos tickets from a domain-joined Linux host
entries.detail: Domain-joined Linux boxes authenticate to Active Directory with Kerberos, so a foothold on one often hands you other users' tickets. Harvest the ccache files in /tmp and the keytab files on disk, import them with kinit, and reuse them with -k against the domain — frequently a straight line from a low-priv shell to a Domain Admin on the DC.
entries.words: When to reach for it Confirm the host talks to Active Directory Find tickets: ccache and keytab files Import a ticket and reuse it Convert between Linux and Windows formats Workflow Notes

entries.label: PassTheCert: Certificate auth over LDAPS when PKINIT is unavailable
entries.detail: The fallback for when you hold a certificate but the KDC will not accept it for PKINIT pre-authentication — often a missing EKU on a domain controller's cert. PassTheCert authenticates to LDAPS with the certificate instead and performs directory attacks directly: grant yourself DCSync, reset a password, or add a computer.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: PEASS-ng (linPEAS / winPEAS): Privilege escalation enumeration
entries.detail: The privilege-escalation scouts. linPEAS and winPEAS enumerate a host for local privesc routes: weak permissions, stored credentials, misconfigured services, sudo and SUID, scheduled tasks: and colour-code the most promising findings. Run one the moment you land a shell.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: PKINITtools: PKINIT TGTs from certificates on Linux
entries.detail: dirkjanm's Python toolkit for the PKINIT side of Kerberos. gettgtpkinit exchanges an X.509 certificate for a TGT, getnthash recovers the account's NT hash from that TGT, and gets4uticket does S4U for constrained-delegation abuse. The engine behind every Pass-the-Certificate and Shadow Credentials attack from Linux.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key tools and flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: PowerUp / SharpUp: Windows privilege-escalation checks
entries.detail: Hunts the common misconfigurations that let a normal user become SYSTEM on Windows — unquoted service paths, weak service and binary permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated, modifiable scheduled tasks and registry autoruns — and, with PowerUp, can abuse them directly. SharpUp is the compiled C# version for when PowerShell is blocked.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: PowerView: AD situational awareness from a Windows host
entries.detail: The PowerShell workhorse for Active Directory enumeration from a Windows foothold. It wraps LDAP in friendly cmdlets — users, groups, computers, GPOs, ACLs, sessions and local-admin access — so you can map attack paths by hand when BloodHound is not an option. Part of PowerSploit; the go-to for living-off-the-land AD recon.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: pspy: Watching processes and cron without root
entries.detail: Watches every process start on a Linux host in real time, with no root and no need to read restricted files. It is how you catch root's cron jobs, scheduled scripts and service restarts as they fire — the commands, their arguments and any secrets passed on the command line. Often the finding that turns a user shell into root.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: pypykatz: Parsing Windows secrets from dumps on Linux
entries.detail: A pure-Python reimplementation of Mimikatz's parsing. It extracts credentials from an LSASS minidump, the SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY registry hives, and DPAPI blobs — all offline, on your Linux box, away from the target's defences. Dump the material with a living-off-the-land tool, then let pypykatz read it.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: pywhisker: Writing Shadow Credentials from Linux
entries.detail: The Linux tool for the Shadow Credentials attack. Given write access to a victim's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute, pywhisker adds a key credential you control and exports a PFX — which you then exchange for the victim's Kerberos TGT via PKINIT. A quiet, reversible takeover that needs no password reset.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: RDP access: Interactive access over 3389
entries.detail: With a credential and 3389 open, RDP gives a full interactive desktop, the quiet way onto a Windows host when WinRM is shut. xfreerdp drives it from Linux, including pass-the-hash where Restricted Admin is on, with a shared drive to move files.
entries.words: When to reach for it Connect from Linux Move files and clipboard Notes

entries.label: Rubeus: Kerberos abuse toolkit (Windows)
entries.detail: The Kerberos Swiss army knife on Windows. Request and dump tickets, Kerberoast and AS-REP roast, turn a hash or key into a TGT (OverPass-the-Hash), and import tickets for Pass-the-Ticket. The Windows counterpart to Impacket's Kerberos tools.
entries.words: When to reach for it Harvest and roast Request a ticket (OverPass-the-Hash / Pass-the-Key) Pass the Ticket Notes

entries.label: Seatbelt: Windows host survey for post-exploitation
entries.detail: A C# host survey that gathers the security-relevant facts about a Windows box — token privileges, UAC and defences, stored credentials and tokens, user activity, network state and local secrets. Where winPEAS scores privesc, Seatbelt answers "what is this machine and what is on it", fast and in one binary.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: secretsdump: Impacket credential dumping
entries.detail: Impacket's one-stop credential dumper. Pull the local SAM and LSA secrets, DCSync the domain hashes from a DC, or parse saved registry hives and NTDS.dit offline. The Linux counterpart to running Mimikatz on the box, and the usual source of the hashes you then crack or pass.
entries.words: When to reach for it Remote: local SAM and LSA DCSync: domain hashes from a Domain Controller Offline: saved hives or NTDS.dit Notes

entries.label: Shadow Credentials: Account takeover via msDS-KeyCredentialLink
entries.detail: If you can write to a victim's msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute, you can add your own public key as an alternate credential and then authenticate as them with the matching certificate via PKINIT. A quiet, reversible takeover that needs no password reset — the go-to when BloodHound shows an AddKeyCredentialLink edge.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Snaffler: Hunting secrets across domain shares
entries.detail: Crawls every readable SMB share in a domain and surfaces the files worth reading — configs, scripts, keys, password-looking strings and known-sensitive filenames — ranked by how interesting they are. The scalable way to find the one credential sitting on a file server among thousands of boring files.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Windows privilege escalation: Local admin / SYSTEM on Windows
entries.detail: Routes from a user shell to SYSTEM on Windows: token privileges, weak services, unquoted paths, AlwaysInstallElevated, stored credentials and autoruns. Enumerate, then take the one that fits.
entries.words: Enumerate Common wins Stored credentials Notes

entries.label: xfreerdp: RDP client (connect, Pass-the-Hash, mount)
entries.detail: The Linux RDP client of choice. Connect with a password or Pass-the-Hash, mount a local drive for file transfer, share the clipboard, and skip the certificate warning. The quiet GUI route onto a Windows host once you have a credential or a hash.
entries.words: When to reach for it Connect Pass the Hash (Restricted Admin) Transfer files and clipboard Useful flags Notes

entries.label: Chisel: Tunnelling and pivoting
entries.detail: A fast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP, in a single Go binary for every platform. Builds a SOCKS proxy or port-forward through a compromised host so your tools on the outside can reach an internal network you otherwise cannot touch.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: File transfer (web, SMB, FTP): Getting files on and off a host
entries.detail: The everyday ways to move a tool onto a target or pull loot back, over HTTP, SMB or FTP. Host a server on your box, then fetch or push from the target with what it already has.
entries.words: Pick a channel Host a server on your attacking box Windows: download Windows: upload Linux: download and upload Base64 copy and paste (no network) Notes

entries.label: File transfer with code: Download and upload with a language runtime
entries.detail: When the usual tools are missing but a language runtime is present. Python, PHP, Ruby, Perl, JavaScript and VBScript all run one-line downloaders, and Python also uploads.
entries.words: When to reach for it Download Windows with JavaScript or VBScript Upload with Python Notes

entries.label: Hashcat / John the Ripper: Offline hash cracking
entries.detail: Where captured hashes turn into passwords. Hashcat is the GPU workhorse; John covers odd formats, CPU cracking and the *2john extractors. The end of the credential-capture chain: Responder loot, Kerberoast tickets, shadow and KeePass files all land here.
entries.words: When to reach for it Identify the hash first Hashcat: key flags Hashcat: commands John: modes, flags and the *2john tools Workflow Notes

entries.label: ligolo-ng: Tunnelling and pivoting
entries.detail: A VPN-style pivot. Instead of a SOCKS proxy and proxychains, it stands up a tun interface so your tools reach the internal network directly, at native speed and with no wrapper. The current go-to for pivoting once you have a foothold.
entries.words: When to reach for it The two pieces Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Living off the land (LOLBAS / GTFOBins): Transfers with trusted built-in binaries
entries.detail: Using signed, already-installed binaries to pull or push files, so nothing new lands on disk and application whitelisting is less likely to block you. The LOLBAS (Windows) and GTFOBins (Linux) projects catalogue them.
entries.words: The idea Windows download Windows upload Linux (GTFOBins), openssl as an nc-style transfer Notes

entries.label: Metasploit Framework: Exploitation framework
entries.detail: The exploitation framework: a searchable library of exploits and payloads, the multi/handler that catches shells, Meterpreter for post-exploitation, and routing for pivoting. The hub that ties weaponisation, exploitation and C2 together.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Payloads: staged vs stageless Meterpreter: core post-exploitation Privilege escalation Credentials Pivoting Persistence (authorised engagements only) Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: msfvenom: Payload generation
entries.detail: The Metasploit payload generator. Produces reverse and bind shells in the format the target can run: exe, elf, war, aspx, raw shellcode: ready to pair with a listener. The standard way to make a payload for an authorised test.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: netcat: The TCP/UDP swiss-army knife
entries.detail: Reads and writes raw TCP/UDP connections, which makes it the default tool for a dozen small jobs: catching a reverse shell, grabbing a service banner, a quick port check, and moving a file when nothing fancier is available. The piece of plumbing every engagement leans on.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Pivoting and tunnelling: Reaching an internal network through a foothold
entries.detail: Using a compromised host to reach the network behind it. SSH port forwards, a SOCKS proxy through proxychains, or a userland VPN with Ligolo-ng, so your tools on the outside hit internal targets.
entries.words: SSH forwards proxychains Ligolo-ng (userland VPN, no proxychains) Notes

entries.label: Protected and evasive transfers: Encrypting files and blending in
entries.detail: Encrypt sensitive data before it moves, and change the user agent so a transfer does not stand out. For exfil during an authorised test and for handling client data responsibly.
entries.words: Encrypt before it moves Blend the transfer in Notes

entries.label: proxychains: Routing tools through a SOCKS pivot
entries.detail: Forces an ordinary tool's TCP connections through a SOCKS proxy, so nmap, smbclient or Impacket on your box can reach a network they have no route to. It is the glue between a tunnel — a Chisel, ligolo-ng or SSH SOCKS proxy on a foothold — and the tools you already know. No tool rewrites, just a prefix.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Reverse shells: Getting a shell back
entries.detail: Turning code execution into an interactive shell on your machine. Start a listener, fire a one-liner on the target, and catch the connection. The payloads that work when you already have a way to run a command.
entries.words: When to reach for it Start a listener Linux target one-liners Windows target one-liners Notes

entries.label: Shell upgrade (TTY): Stabilising a caught shell
entries.detail: Turning the dumb shell you just caught into a usable one: job control, tab completion, arrow keys, and a window size that does not break full-screen tools. The first thing to do after catching a Linux reverse shell.
entries.words: When to reach for it Linux: full TTY upgrade Linux: quick improvements (when a full TTY will not cooperate) Windows Notes

entries.label: socat: Relays, port forwards and better shells
entries.detail: A multi-tool for moving bytes between two endpoints — sockets, files, ttys, pipes. On an engagement it catches and upgrades shells to a fully interactive TTY, relays a connection through a foothold, forwards a port, and moves files. When netcat runs out of options, socat usually has one.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: sshuttle: Tunnelling and pivoting
entries.detail: A poor man's VPN over plain SSH. Point it at a host you can SSH to and it routes a whole subnet through that host, so your tools reach the internal network with no proxychains. Reach for it when you have SSH to a dual-homed box and want a quick pivot.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Transfer when the web is blocked: Netcat, /dev/tcp, RDP and WinRM
entries.detail: Moving files without an HTTP or SMB server: a raw Netcat or /dev/tcp pipe, an RDP drive mount, or a PowerShell Remoting session. For when outbound web and SMB are filtered.
terms: transfer when the web is blocked
entries.words: Netcat / Ncat Bash /dev/tcp (no nc on the target) PowerShell Remoting (WinRM) RDP drive mount Notes

entries.label: Wordlists and rules: Crafting lists tuned to the target
entries.detail: A generic list wastes guesses; a list built from the target lands. Scrape words off the company site, generate candidate usernames from names, mangle a seed list with rules, and build masks that match the password policy you pulled.
entries.words: When to reach for it Scrape and generate Mangle with rules Masks for a known policy Notes
